title_ar: الضوابط الشرعية لفهم الكتاب والسنة الجزء الأول
title_en: The Legal Controls for Understanding the Book and the Sunnah — Part One
body_ar:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين، وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين، السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته.

أما بعد فإن الله أرسل إلينا محمدا (ص) بهذا الدين مظروفا في هذين الوحيين الثقلين كتاب الله وسنة محمد (ص) وهما بلسان عربي مبين، وقد نوع الله سبحانه وتعالى دلالاتهما، فكانت دلالات القرآن متباينة منه ما هو واضح الدلالة ومنه ما هو خفي الدلالة، وواضح الدلالة منه ما هو محكم ومنه ما هو مفسر ومنه ما هو مبين ومنه ما هو ظاهر ومنه ما هو نص، وخفي الدلالة منه ما هو مجمل ومنه ما هو مشكل ومنه ما هو خفي ومنه ما هو متشابه..
body_en:
In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds. I pray for blessing and peace upon the one who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions and all who are guided by his guidance and follow his practice until the Day of Judgement. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings.

To proceed: God sent Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, to us with this religion, contained within these two weighty revelations — the Book of God and the sunnah of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him — and the two of them are in clear Arabic speech. God, glorified and exalted, made their modes of signification various. The Qur'an's modes of signification are of different kinds: some of it is clear in what it signifies and some of it is obscure in what it signifies. What is clear in signification includes what is of clear import (muḥkam), what is expounded (mufassar), what is clarified (mubayyan), what is of apparent meaning (ẓāhir), and what is an explicit text (naṣṣ). What is obscure in signification includes what is unelaborated (mujmal), what is problematic (mushkil), what is hidden (khafī), and what is of ambiguous import (mutashābih)..

flags.arabic: محكم … مفسر … مبين … ظاهر … نص … مجمل … مشكل … خفي … متشابه
flags.context: the ninefold classification of the modes of signification of a text
options: render each with the glossary's English and the Arabic in brackets, as done here
leave the nine terms in transliteration only
flags.note: IMPORTANT FOR ATTRIBUTION. This ninefold scheme — five degrees of clarity, four of obscurity — is the HANAFI classification of dalālāt, not the Maliki or Shafi'i one, which works with a shorter list. The Sheikh presents it here without saying whose it is, and a reader unfamiliar with the field will take it for the scheme simply. Four of the nine terms are already fixed in the glossary (muḥkam, mubayyan, mujmal, mutashābih, ẓāhir, naṣṣ) and have been used as fixed; mufassar, mushkil and khafī are not yet in the glossary and the renderings here are provisional. A reviewer should confirm all three and add them.

options: end the English where the Arabic ends
flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY — STYLE GUIDE §9. The page publishes the opening of the lecture and breaks off on a double full stop, immediately after the list of terms and before a single one of them is explained. The title promises the controls for understanding the Book and the sunnah; the excerpt supplies a bare taxonomy. The full lecture is behind the .docx download.

flags.context: the description of how the religion is contained in the two revelations
options: contained within these two weighty revelations
enclosed as in a vessel within these two weighty revelations
wrapped up in these two great revelations
flags.note: maẓrūf is from ẓarf, a container or vessel, and the Sheikh is using a deliberate figure: the religion is the contents, the two revelations the vessel. 'Contained' is flatter than the Arabic; option 2 keeps the figure at the cost of some weight. al-thaqalayn, 'the two weighty things', also echoes the well-known report about what the Prophet left behind, which the Sheikh does not quote here.

The opening is the khuṭbat al-ḥājah, the standard formula with which the Sheikh begins a lecture. It is rendered in full rather than abbreviated, since it is part of the text as published.

The source writes the eulogy after the Prophet's name sometimes in full (صلى الله عليه وسلم) and sometimes as the abbreviation (ص). Both are rendered in English as 'peace and blessings be upon him'; the source form is preserved in body_ar.

'Modes of signification' renders dalālāt, the technical term of legal theory for the ways a text indicates a ruling. It is not in the glossary and should be added; the rendering here is provisional.
This record is Part One of a two-part lecture; Part Two is record 580, which is also an excerpt and which begins in mid-sentence.
